rationale: If the Iraqi Government goes through with the threat to expel foreign troops, and/or if militia attacks against foreign security personnel increase, foreign troops are likely to leave Iraq or see their capacity to operate severely limited. The number of ISIS attacks is likely to spike with consequent rising protection concerns for the local residents.

title: The US/Israel–Iran escalation affecting the Strait of Hormuz drives conflict, food insecurity, livelihood collapse, and protection risks in Iraq
rationale: A US–Iran confrontation triggered by a ten-day ultimatum issued by the US administration for Iran to reach a nuclear and regional agreement (placing a potential military trigger in late February or early March 2026) could increase humanitarian needs in Iraq through two compounding mechanisms: direct Iranian proxy escalation via the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) and broader regional economic disruption, including potential closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Following the fall of Bashar Al Assad's regime in Syria and Israel's weakening of Hezbollah in Lebanon and Syria, Iraq has become a significant regional asset for Iran. The PMF, an official Iraqi security institution composed largely of Iran-backed militias, represents Iran's likely vector for retaliation against US interests in Iraq. Kata'ib Hezbollah, the largest militia within the PMF, has publicly warned of military response if Iran is attacked. Iraq's political trajectory compounds this risk. Government formation remains contested between the US administration and Iraq's Coordination Framework over the composition of leaders
expectedImpact: A US–Iran confrontation involving the disruption or closure of the Strait of Hormuz would threaten Iraq's ability to sustain basic humanitarian services, with IDPs most severely affected. The collapse or severe disruption of the PDS would increase acute food insecurity, particularly among the approximately one million IDPs in the country. title: Contested electoral process ahead of Côte d'Ivoire’s October 2025 elections leads to political violence and protection risks
rationale: Côte d’Ivoire is preparing for presidential elections scheduled for 25 October 2025. Although recent elections have been relatively peaceful, the political environment is becoming increasingly tense. The Independent Electoral Commission (CEI) released the final electoral roll on 4 June, confirming the exclusion of four prominent opposition leaders: Laurent Gbagbo, Tidjane Thiam, Charles Blé Goudé, and Guillaume Soro. While Thiam was excluded based on nationality concerns, the others were barred because of past judicial convictions. All four are also prohibited from voting. The exclusion of these high-profile figures has triggered strong criticism from their parties, which have withdrawn from the CEI and denounced a lack of institutional independence. Some, such as Thiam and his party, have appealed to international bodies such as the UNHRC. Others, including former first lady Simone Gbagbo, have warned that the conditions are not in place for peaceful elections. Cuts in humanitarian aid have already led to reductions in food rations, the closure of essential services, and growing frustration among both refugees and host communities. In 2025, WFP was only able to provide 60% of the minimum food basket by midyear, with responders reporting critical gaps in healthcare, education, and WASH services. The camps, which host more than 600,000 refugees, are still absorbing new displacements from conflict-affected areas of Ethiopia, Somalia, and Sudan. These arrivals further strain already limited resources and contribute to tensions over land, water, and security. Escalating tensions have already led to ethnic clashes, protests, and police interventions within camps including Kakuma and Dadaab. title: Forecast El Niño conditions threaten crop production and worsen food insecurity in Kenya
rationale: El Niño conditions are forecast to develop by July 2026 and strengthen through the second half of the year. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates a 61% probability of El Niño from May–July, rising to 87–92% between July 2026 and January 2027. The Intergovernmental Authority on Development Climate Prediction and Applications Centre forecasts below-normal June–September (JJAS) rainfall across western and northern Kenya alongside above-normal temperatures nationwide, closely resembling the 2023 El Niño, when below-normal JJAS rainfall affected western Kenya. The forecast threatens Kenya's principal food-producing areas during a critical stage of the long rains season. Over 70% of the country's annual crop production depends on the long rains, which extend into August–September in the North Rift and western Kenya. These areas had already recorded below-average rainfall in April and early May despite favourable national rainfall totals. title: A rising number of Syrian refugees opt for an unsafe return to Syria to avoid a deepening economic crisis in Lebanon and the repercussions of the 2020 Beirut explosion
rationale: Inflation, rising prices, and the depreciation of the Lebanese lira threaten the livelihoods of Syrian refugees, who struggle to survive on cash assistance (delivered in Lebanese liras) or receive low to no salary from their employers in the informal sector. Because of these factors, as well as Lebanese governmental policies on return, an increasing number of refugees might opt for an unsafe return to Syria. While the severity of people’s needs has worsened, during 2020, the number of voluntary refugees returning to Syria was only 9,351 – half of the figure registered in 2019. The refugees' decisions to return to Syria were influenced mainly by the security and safety situation, economic growth, public service availability, and personal relationships in their place of origin, while refugees’ poor living conditions in Lebanon were less likely to be an influence. Unless the situation significantly improves in Syria, refugees are unlikely to return.

title: Diplomatic tensions between Lebanon and the Gulf states affect Lebanon's economy and aggravate humanitarian needs
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: Political tension between Lebanon and some Gulf countries caused a risk of deterioration of Lebanon’s economy and increased humanitarian needs across all sectors for the most vulnerable. The diplomatic crisis threatened the job security of the Lebanese diaspora in the Gulf states, potentially affecting remittances and decreasing the flow of foreign currency into Lebanon, as Lebanon had been exporting basic goods and materials to some Gulf states. Following Information Minister George Kordahi’s comments on the role of the United Arab Emirates and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in the war in Yemen – including implications that the Houthis had the right to defend themselves against foreign attacks – Bahrain, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates expelled Lebanese ambassadors from their countries. The Gulf states perceived these comments as antagonising. Saudi Arabia also banned Lebanese imports to the kingdom and asked the minister to resign as a condition to lift the ban.

Israel carried out at least two airstrikes in Ghaziyeh town, five kilometres outside a key Lebanese city (Saida), on 19 February. This attack was considered the largest airstrikes carried out near a major population centre since 8 October. A factory producing electrical generators was targeted. On 26 February, an Israeli air strike targeted the outskirts of Buday village near Baalbek city, eastern Lebanon for the first time since 8 October 2023. The attacks targeted a convoy of trucks carrying food, killing at least two people. Hezbollah has also been responding with expanding the geographical area targeted in Israel, increasing the likelihood of further clashes and impacting more areas in Lebanon.

title: El Niño drives drought conditions, increasing food insecurity and heightening humanitarian needs in Madagascar in 2027
rationale: Current models indicate a very high probability for El Niño to develop by July 2026 and persist into early 2027. In Madagascar, El Niño typically drives precipitation and temperature anomalies, with dry conditions in southern parts of the country and heavy rainfall in the north and east. title: La Niña-driven above-normal rainfall and enhanced cyclonic activity in the Philippines cause widespread flooding, agricultural damage, and displacement
rationale: La Niña arrived in the Philippines in October 2025 and is likely to persist until February–March 2026. La Niña events have typically been linked to a higher frequency of tropical cyclones late in the year, along with increased rainfall and flood risk across much of the country. Current seasonal forecasts anticipate a high probability of above-average precipitation and above-average temperatures between November 2025 and March 2026. This indicates that between late 2025 and early 2026, the country could face compounding hazards, including storms and intense northeast monsoon rains, which may cause widespread flooding and landslides, especially across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao. Coastal and riverine communities in the Bicol region, Eastern Visayas, and Mindanao are particularly exposed, while informal urban settlements in Metro Manila and Cebu face a high risk of waterlogging and infrastructure collapse. The agreement has also deepened rifts within the main opposition coalition, the Forum for National Salvation, with former president Sharif Sheikh Ahmed insisting that the prevailing insecurity makes the implementation of such extensive electoral reforms unfeasible. Tensions have also emerged between SAF and factions linked to JEM, the Joint Forces, and other groups present in civilian and commercial areas in Khartoum. US designation and sanctions linked to the Sudanese Muslim Brotherhood and Al Baraa Bin Malik Brigade add further external pressure on SAF to disengage from these groups. Clashes broke out on 28 April in the predominantly Druze districts of Jaramana and Sahnaya in Damascus as local Druze fighters exchanged fire with Sunni gunmen. rationale: The Syria–Lebanon border remains a key smuggling corridor for fuel, drugs (especially Captagon), and weapons, primarily from Syria to Lebanon, often facilitated by networks linked to Hezbollah and Iran-backed militias. As of April 2024, Al Hol hosts 42,000 people, and as of December 2024 Al Roj hosts over 2,600 people. title: Water scarcity, especially in northeast and northwest Syria result in livelihoods and services’ disruptions, reduced food production and protests
type: Marked deterioration in an existing crisis
rationale: As of February 2025, about 13.6 million Syrians lack access to safe water and sanitation. Ongoing electricity and fuel shortages have crippled water pumps and treatment plants, exacerbating water rationing and existing sanitation problems and driving disease outbreaks. Syria and the region experienced an exceptionally dry winter and spring in 2024/2025, with significantly below-average rainfall and higher temperatures. title: Spreading of the violent insurgency of Cabo Delgado into the Tanzanian territory.
rationale: There has been no violent attacks taking place in Tanzania since the entry of this risk in November. On 14 October, some 300 insurgents from Mozambique attacked Kitaya, a riverside border village in the Mtwara region. The Tanzanian authorities acknowledged for the first time an attack in Tanzania carried out by insurgents coming from the neighbouring country. In November 2020, Tanzania and Mozambique have signed a memorandum of understanding aimed to join forces against ISIL-linked fighters in Cabo Delgado. Recently raids have been carried out in Tanzanian villages near the border and many fighters are believed to come from Tanzania. The population of Mtwara region (which borders with Cabo Delgado) is over 1,270,000 people. rationale: Since 2010, the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events in Tanzania have increased, including heavy rainfall, flooding, and landslides. Past floods in Kilimanjaro, Kilombero, Manyara, Mbeya, Morogoro, and Rufiji regions have had significant humanitarian and socioeconomic impacts, including loss of life, property destruction, displacement, and economic decline.
